links.outcome: Radiologist diagnostic accuracy with vs without LLM support by explanation format; adherence/overreliance
links.effect: Chain-of-thought improved accuracy 12.2 pp vs control (P=0.001); standard output +5.0 pp (P=0.150) and differential diagnosis +2.5 pp (P=0.446) not significant vs control. Differential diagnosis group over-adhered to wrong advice (63.3-80.0%).
links.quote: Physicians in the chain-of-thought group performed best with a 12.2 percentage point improvement over the control group (95% CI = [5.3, 19.2], P = 0.001).

links.outcome: Human-AI team accuracy across LLM output formats versus control, in vignette workflow
links.effect: Effectiveness of LLM support varied by format: chain-of-thought +12.2 pp vs control, +7.2 pp vs standard, +9.7 pp vs differential diagnosis; other formats were not significantly better than control.
links.quote: Our experiment demonstrates that the format of explanation plays a surprisingly important role in the effectiveness of LLM support.

links.outcome: Adherence to incorrect LLM diagnoses (automation bias) by explanation format
links.effect: When the LLM diagnosis was incorrect, adherence was 63.3% and 80.0% in the differential diagnosis group vs 25.0% and 30.6% in standard output and 30.4% in chain-of-thought.
links.quote: Thus, physicians in the differential diagnosis group appeared more inclined to follow the LLM-generated advice even when it was wrong.

links.outcome: Whether output presentation format promotes selective adherence and overriding of incorrect LLM advice
links.effect: Chain-of-thought explanations led to more selective adherence than differential diagnosis, with physicians more likely to follow correct advice and override incorrect advice; accuracy +9.7 pp vs differential diagnosis (P=0.004).
links.quote: Conversely, the chain-of-thought explanation (in comparison to the differential diagnosis) led to more selective adherence, with physicians being more likely to follow correct LLM advice and to override incorrect LLM advice.

links.outcome: Effect of LLM explanation formats on clinicians' diagnostic accuracy
links.effect: Chain-of-thought explanations improved accuracy 12.2 pp vs control (P=0.001) and 7.2 pp vs standard output without explanation (P=0.040); differential diagnosis was not significantly better than control.
links.quote: The chain-of-thought explanations are also superior to the standard output without explanation ( + 7.2%; P = 0.040) and the differential diagnosis format ( + 9.7%; P = 0.004).

links.outcome: Accuracy with differential-diagnosis (unranked-style multiple options) format versus other formats
links.effect: Differential diagnosis format showed no significant gain over control (+2.5 pp, P=0.446) and was outperformed by chain-of-thought by 9.7 pp (P=0.004); it induced over-adherence to incorrect advice.
links.quote: Differential diagnoses, by contrast, enumerate multiple options—here, five possibilities—without providing explicit reasoning for each.

links.outcome: GPT-4 diagnostic accuracy on radiology cases
links.effect: LLM achieved moderate accuracy overall: standard 75%; differential 65% top-1 and 80% top-5; chain-of-thought 80%. Radiologists were outperformed by the LLM alone.
links.quote: The LLM achieved moderate diagnostic accuracy overall (standard output: 75%; differential diagnosis: 65% for the top-1 answer and 80% for the top-5 answers; chain-of-thought: 80%; Supplementary Fig. 1 ), which underscores the need for careful evaluation of LLM outputs and which further implies that the selected patient cases were challenging for the model.

unlisted_practices: Selecting LLM explanation format (chain-of-thought vs differential diagnosis vs standard output) to improve clinician diagnostic accuracy

links.outcome: training-data memorization of cases
links.effect: Ratcliff/Obershelp 0.049 and BLEU 0.006; Wikipedia BLEU 0.048, 8-fold higher.
links.quote: Average similarity scores across all patient cases were consistently low (Ratcliff/Obershelp: 0.049, BLEU: 0.006).

links.outcome: LLM diagnostic accuracy
links.effect: Standard output 75%; differential 65% top-1, 80% top-5; chain-of-thought 80%.
links.quote: The LLM achieved moderate diagnostic accuracy overall (standard output: 75%; differential diagnosis: 65% for the top-1 answer and 80% for the top-5 answers; chain-of-thought: 80%; Supplementary Fig. 1 ), which underscores the need for careful evaluation of LLM outputs and which further implies that the selected patient cases were challenging for the model.

links.outcome: human-AI diagnostic accuracy
links.effect: Standard +5.0 points (P=0.150), differential +2.5 (P=0.446), chain-of-thought +12.2 (P=0.001) vs control.
links.quote: Physicians augmented with LLM advice outperformed those in the control group without LLM advice (Fig. 2 for statistical comparisons based on one-sided Welch’s t -tests).

links.outcome: selective adherence and overriding
links.effect: Correct advice adherence CoT 90.8%/94.0%; incorrect advice adherence CoT 30.4% vs differential 63.3%/80.0%.
links.quote: Conversely, the chain-of-thought explanation (in comparison to the differential diagnosis) led to more selective adherence, with physicians being more likely to follow correct LLM advice and to override incorrect LLM advice.

links.outcome: over-adherence to incorrect advice
links.effect: Differential-diagnosis adherence to incorrect diagnoses was 63.3%/80.0%, exceeding standard 25.0%/30.6% and chain-of-thought 30.4%.
links.quote: When the LLM-generated diagnosis was incorrect (Fig. 3 , right column), adherence was highest in the differential diagnosis group irrespective of the correctness of the explanation (adherence for incorrect diagnosis but correct explanation: 63.3%; adherence for incorrect diagnosis and incorrect explanation: 80.0%), which also exceeded that of the standard output group (25.0% and 30.6%, respectively) and the chain-of-thought group (adherence for incorrect diagnosis and incorrect explanation: 30.4%).

links.outcome: radiologists' diagnostic accuracy
links.effect: Chain-of-thought +12.2 points vs control; +7.2 vs standard; +9.7 vs differential.
links.quote: Physicians in the chain-of-thought group performed best with a 12.2 percentage point improvement over the control group (95% CI = [5.3, 19.2], P = 0.001).

links.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of radiologists across LLM explanation formats
links.effect: Chain-of-thought explanations improved diagnostic accuracy by 7.2 percentage points (95% CI [0.3, 14.2], P = 0.040) over standard output without explanation and 9.7 percentage points (95% CI [3.2, 16.3], P = 0.004) over differential diagnosis.
links.quote: Separate comparisons for the chain-of-thought versus standard condition and chain-of-thought versus differential diagnosis condition showed improvements in the outcome measure by 7.2 percentage points (95% CI = [0.3, 14.2], P = 0.040) and 9.7 percentage points (95% CI = [3.2, 16.3], P = 0.004), respectively, which confirms that the chain-of-thought condition performed best (Supplementary Table 8 ).

links.outcome: Radiologist adherence to incorrect LLM-generated diagnoses
links.effect: When LLM diagnosis was incorrect, adherence was 63.3% to 80.0% with differential diagnosis, 25.0% to 30.6% with standard output, and 30.4% with chain-of-thought.
links.quote: When the LLM-generated diagnosis was incorrect (Fig. 3 , right column), adherence was highest in the differential diagnosis group irrespective of the correctness of the explanation (adherence for incorrect diagnosis but correct explanation: 63.3%; adherence for incorrect diagnosis and incorrect explanation: 80.0%), which also exceeded that of the standard output group (25.0% and 30.6%, respectively) and the chain-of-thought group (adherence for incorrect diagnosis and incorrect explanation: 30.4%).

screen.practice: LLM explanation format (chain-of-thought vs differential vs standard output)
screen.reason: This study experimentally evaluates the effect of different LLM explanation formats (such as chain-of-thought reasoning versus standard diagnostic output) on radiologists' diagnostic decision-making across clinical vignettes.

primary.practice: explanation formatting (chain-of-thought vs standard vs differential diagnosis)
